Hi! I'm completely new to this and don't know where to start, can you guide me?
Welcome to roses, and welcome to Heirloom – I’m excited you’re getting started!
Here’s a simple way to start without feeling overwhelmed:
Pick roses that will thrive where you live
At the top of our website you’ll see a place to choose your hardiness zone (for example, Zone 6, Zone 7, etc.). Select your zone and the site will show roses that are suited to your climate.
You can then use filters under “Shop All Roses” to sort by color, fragrance, type (like climbers or shrubs), and more.
Know what you’re buying
We sell premium own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil (not bare-root). That means the rose grows on its own roots, which tends to make it longer-lived and easier to recover if it gets stressed.
All roses need to be grown outdoors, in at least 6 hours of direct sun per day if possible.
Learn the basics of planting and care Our how-to guides are a great place to begin:
Main how-to library: https://heirloomroses.com/blogs/how-to-articles

turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break it down simply.

I’ll explain the main choices you’ll see when you shop for roses on our site and what they mean.

Hardiness zone (where the rose can live)
This is about winter cold.
At the top of the website you can pick your “zone” (for example, Zone 5, Zone 7).
Once you choose it, the site shows roses that should handle your climate.
Rose type (shape and how it grows) Under Shop All Roses, you can filter by type. The main ones are:
Hybrid tea: Classic long-stemmed roses, usually one big bloom per stem. Great for cutting.
Shrub/bush roses: Full, bushy plants with lots of blooms. Good for beds and borders.
Climbing roses: Long canes you tie to a trellis, fence, or arbor.
Groundcover/landscape: Low, spreading roses that cover an area.
Color
You can pick colors like red, pink, white, yellow, orange, purple, or mixed/bi-color.
This just helps you match your garden style.
Fragrance
You can choose stronger fragrance or lighter fragrance.
If scent is important to you, turn this filter on and pick roses with good fragrance.
Blooming habit (how often they bloom) Look for filters like:
Repeat/rebloom: Roses that bloom, rest, then bloom again through the season.
Continuous: Roses that tend to keep blooming almost nonstop in the season.

For example: If you want roses that bloom more than once, use the “rebloom” filter.

Sun / shade tolerance
Full sun: Needs about 6 or more hours of direct sun a day. Most roses like this.
Partial shade / shade tolerant: Can handle around 4 or more hours of sun, or a bit more shade.
Thorns
You can filter for “thornless” or “nearly thornless” if you want something easier to handle.
How to use the filters on the site
On a computer: When you’re on a rose listing page, the filters are on the left-hand side. Click the sections (like Color, Type, Rebloom) to open them, then check what you want.
On a phone or tablet: Look for a “Filter” or similar button near the top of the product list. Tap it, choose your options, then apply.

turns.replyText:
Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. For a beginner, you really only need a few basics.

The rose itself
Our roses are premium own-root plants that arrive in 1-gallon containers with soil, ready to plant outdoors.
Choose a spot with at least 6 hours of sun and good drainage.
Helpful (optional) soil amendments You can plant without these, but they make it easier for the rose to settle in and grow strong roots:
Bone meal: Supports root development.
Cow manure: Adds long-lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Loosens and aerates soil and can also be used as a top dressing to protect roots.
Worm castings: Gentle nutrients and better soil structure.
Fertilizer (this one is important) Fertilizing is needed for good growth and blooms.
We offer several options like OmniMeal and Founders Fish Fertilizer, but you can use any good rose fertilizer you prefer.
For the first year, a liquid fertilizer is usually easiest for beginners, as it is simple to apply and absorbs quickly.
Simple tools You do not need anything fancy to start. Just:
A hand trowel or shovel for digging the planting hole.
Pruners for trimming canes and deadheading (removing spent flowers) later on.
A quick how-to guide When you are ready to plant, this step-by-step article is very helpful:
Planting roses: https://heirloomroses.com/blogs/how-to-articles/planting-roses
